body_text: Code Enforcement Software for Multirole Government Teams August 13, 2026 by Julie Crump The Code Enforcement Complaint That Lands on an Already Full Plate In many local governments, the person fielding a new code complaint in the morning is the same person who pulled permit records for a council report the afternoon before. Code enforcement is rarely a single-role job. The staff who handle complaints also field questions about open permits, manage abatement timelines, and generate documentation for cases that are moving through the process, all at the same time. On a normal week, someone handling code enforcement alongside other responsibilities might: Receive a complaint and research current parcel ownership and location details before the case can move forward Drive to the property, document conditions on-site, and re-enter that information back at the office Draft enforcement notices, abatement orders, or other case documents for every active complaint Track deadlines across a dozen open cases while fielding new complaints and covering other departmental work The cases themselves are manageable. It’s the coordination across multiple workstreams that becomes time-consuming. "Our previous software did not meet the department’s needs related to caseload and organization of information. Permitting & Licensing Pro streamlined the process for code enforcement and building permits by giving us a comprehensive way to track cases, permits, and inspections." Cibolo, Texas What Changes When Permitting and Code Enforcement Software Connects Your Workflows When parcel ownership details update automatically, staff can bypass the research step that once preceded every new case. When the system generates enforcement documents from information already in the record, staff are not building each notice from a blank form. When deadline reminders are built into the workflow rather than living in someone’s memory, cases don’t get delayed by competing priorities. These are not dramatic changes on their own. But for a team that is already carrying more than it can reasonably track by hand, they add up. The same number of people can manage a larger caseload without the work piling up in the gaps between visits, documents, and deadlines. When permitting, code enforcement, and case records share the same data, there is also less rekeying between systems. An address looked up for a complaint is the same address tied to the permit history. A case status updated in the field is the same status the office sees when a resident or property owner calls about it. Improving the Experience for the Residents Behind the Code Complaints A code complaint is not an administrative abstraction. Someone filed it because an overgrown lot is a community concern, a vacant structure has been sitting for months, or a neighbor’s property has been in disrepair long enough that it feels like no one is paying attention. When a case moves slowly because ownership research takes time, or a notice goes out late because a deadline got lost, the person who filed the complaint is left wondering whether anything is being done. Faster, more consistent case management is how a department earns the credibility to ask residents to keep using the process. When people trust that a complaint leads somewhere, they file them, and that is how problems get resolved before they compound. How to Start Connecting Code Enforcement Workflows The places where code enforcement slows down are usually easy to identify once you start asking the right questions. How much time goes into researching ownership and location details before a new case can open? How many enforcement documents get produced from scratch that the system could generate automatically? How does the team currently track which cases are approaching a legal deadline? When a complaint comes in while staff are already in the field, what falls behind? The answers often reveal where small process improvements can have the biggest impact and where connected case management can deliver value first. Streamline Code Enforcement With Permitting & Licensing Pro Permitting & Licensing Pro brings complaint intake, case management, document generation, and deadline tracking into one connected platform — so multirole government teams can manage more cases with less manual work . title: Palladyne AI and Orkid Tech Partner to Extend Palladyne™ Pilot and SwarmOS™ Autonomy Platform to Fixed-Wing UAVs
summary: Palladyne AI and Orkid Tech will integrate Pilot and SwarmOS autonomy software with Orkid's NDAA-compliant fixed-wing UAVs for defense and industrial markets.
body_text: Agreement marks Palladyne AI’s first fixed-wing UAV partnership, pairing Orkid Tech’s fielded, NDAA-compliant UAVs with Palladyne AI’s Pilot and SwarmOS software SALT LAKE CITY & DENVER – August 19, 2026 – Palladyne AI Corp. (NASDAQ: PDYN), a U.S.-based defense and industrial technology company delivering embodied AI-powered collaborative autonomy solutions, advanced avionics, precision-manufactured components, UAVs, and advanced aerospace engineering services, and Orkid Tech, a developer of long-range, NDAA-compliant vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), today announced a collaboration to integrate its Palladyne Pilot and SwarmOS autonomy software with Orkid’s fixed-wing UAV platform. The companies intend to develop integrated drone systems for the U.S. Department of War and commercial industrial markets, including oil & gas, power, wildfire management, and public safety, extending Palladyne AI’s Pilot and SwarmOS platform into a new class of aircraft and adding a fixed-wing growth vector to its addressable market. The companies will combine Orkid’s proven, NDAA-compliant VTOL fixed-wing UAV platform with Palladyne AI’s Pilot and SwarmOS autonomy software. Orkid’s UAV takes off and lands without a runway, deploys in minutes, and features modular payload flexibility that can be reconfigured for different sensors depending on the mission. By adding Palladyne Pilot or SwarmOS to the Orkid UAV, the companies will deliver fixed-wing systems that operate autonomously, not simply with automated waypoint following or preprogrammed flight, enabling the aircraft to respond in real-time to evolving circumstances on the ground and in the air. The result is a multi-aircraft swarm that a single pilot can operate while reducing cognitive load. “This is our first partnership focused on bringing SwarmOS to fixed-wing aircraft, and it does so on a proven, fielded platform built for demanding missions,” said Ben Wolff, President and CEO of Palladyne AI. “For defense and industrial customers, it means a team of aircraft that will sense, decide, and act together, delivering sharper ISR in contested environments and faster, more complete inspection coverage for commercial operators. It also represents another step toward scaling Palladyne AI’s hardware-agnostic software model and capturing the commercial deployment opportunities ahead.” “We evaluated a number of different possibilities for enabling autonomy on our UAVs. There is a lot of hype and overpromising when it comes to true autonomy on UAVs, but Palladyne AI is delivering real collaborative autonomy today. We just completed a joint field exercise with Palladyne AI, and we were able to see SwarmOS in action in the hands of soldiers in real-world exercises,” said Santiago Pinzon, CEO and co-founder of Orkid Tech. “The combination of our NDAA-compliant, long-duration, fixed-wing VTOL UAVs with Palladyne AI’s collaborative autonomy software will deliver a compelling capability to both defense and industrial customers.” About Palladyne AI Palladyne AI is a U.S.-based technology company developing patented embodied artificial intelligence, collaborative autonomy solutions, and autonomous systems for defense and industrial markets. Palladyne AI delivers secure, American-developed and operated platforms designed to meet the stringent requirements of U.S. government and public-sector customers, including data sovereignty, security, and compliance. Palladyne AI’s embodied AI is designed to operate in complex, contested, and high-risk environments, enabling distributed tasking, human-on-the-loop decision-making, degraded-communications resilience, and multi-domain coordination. Its platform-agnostic autonomy stack combines real-time sensor fusion, adaptive AI models, and edge-native orchestration to support autonomous and collaborative systems across air, ground, maritime, and industrial domains. For more information about Palladyne AI, including GuideTech and Palladyne Aerospace and Defense, please visit www.palladyneai.com . About Orkid Tech Orkid Tech is a U.S. unmanned aircraft systems company developing and manufacturing long-range, NDAA-compliant fixed-wing VTOL aircraft for defense, public safety, and commercial applications. Orkid’s aircraft combine the endurance and efficiency of fixed-wing flight with runway-independent vertical takeoff and landing, enabling rapid deployment in remote, austere, and operationally complex environments. Designed around a modular, mission-configurable architecture, Orkid platforms support advanced electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR), mapping, LiDAR, and other specialized payloads, as well as satellite-enabled communications for beyond-line-of-sight operations. Orkid systems are designed to support missions including intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), infrastructure inspection, wildfire management, search and rescue, mapping, and other long-duration operations. Orkid Tech is headquartered in Orlando, Florida, with engineering, manufacturing, integration, and operational capabilities supporting customers in the United States and international markets. title: Web Search in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds domain and published date filtering, expands to Europe and Asia Pacific
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Web Search in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds domain and published date filtering, expands to Europe and Asia Pacific
body_text: Web Search in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now supports domain filtering and published-date filtering, giving agents per-request control over which web sources and time windows they search. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the infrastructure to build, connect, and optimize AI agents, and Web Search enables those agents to ground responses in current web data. With runtime domain filtering, agents can narrow search results to trusted sources or block unwanted domains on a per-call basis without requiring admin reconfiguration. Published-date filtering allows agents to constrain results to a specific time window using inclusive from and to date bounds, ensuring responses reflect only timely, relevant content. With this launch, agents can pass include and exclude domain lists and a published-date range directly in each tool call, while admins gain new gateway-level allowlist support and an increased domain cap of up to 100 domains per list. These capabilities are ideal for regulated industries, research workflows, and applications that require strict control over information sources and recency. The Web Search Tool is also expanding to Europe (Ireland) (eu-west-1) and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) (ap-northeast-1), joining the existing US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1) availability. To learn more, read the technical blog about domain and published date filters , and review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product documentation .

title: 4DMT’s 2-year PRISM Data Show Durable Treatment Burden Reduction with 4D-150 in Wet AMD
summary: Two-year PRISM results show 4D-150 gene therapy sustains wet AMD vision while cutting anti-VEGF injections up to 87%, with reassuring safety.
body_text: Two-year follow-up from the Phase 2b PRISM clinical trial continues to support 4D-150, 4D Molecular Therapeutics' (4DMT) investigational gene therapy for wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD) , as a potential single-injection alternative to chronic anti-VEGF dosing.1 The data, with a cutoff of May 18, 2026, were presented in an oral session titled "2-Year Follow Up: PRISM Phase 2b Clinical Trial Evaluating Investigational 4D-150, an Intravitreal Gene Therapy, in a Broad Neovascular AMD Population" by Carl Awh, MD, FASRS, of Tennessee Retina, at the 44th Annual Scientific Meeting of the American Society of Retina Specialists (ASRS) in Montréal.1,2 Sustained vision and anatomic outcomes, sharply reduced injection burden PRISM Phase 2b enrolled 45 patients across two dose levels of a single intravitreal injection of 4D-150—3E10 vg/eye (n=30) and 1E10 vg/eye (n=15)—with 3E10 vg/eye subsequently selected as the dose carried forward into the 4FRONT Phase 3 program .1,3 A recently diagnosed subgroup (diagnosed within 6 months, n=15 at 3E10 vg/eye) was included specifically because it most closely mirrors the treatment-naïve population enrolled in 4FRONT-1 and 4FRONT-2.1 Through 2 years, the company reported consistent maintenance of best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and consistent control of central subfield thickness (CST) on optical coherence tomography, with the dose response favoring the Phase 3 dose holding throughout follow-up. The treatment-burden findings were the headline result: the overall cohort saw a 78% reduction in supplemental injections, averaging 2.7 injections per patient versus a projected 12.0 injections under on-label aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks. In the recently diagnosed subgroup, that reduction reached 87%, with a mean of 1.6 supplemental injections per patient.1 The finding builds on interim results from the same cohort reported at 52 weeks last year and on longer-interval follow-up from the Phase 1/2a portion of PRISM , both of which pointed in the same direction.4,5 On safety, the company said 4D-150 continues to be well tolerated. As previously reported, 2 of 71 patients (2.8%) treated at the Phase 3 dose across the pooled Phase 1/2a and 2b population had 4D-150-related mild (1+) intraocular inflammation within roughly the first 6 months after dosing, described as transient vitreous cells noted at a single timepoint. No new inflammation cases have emerged since, across follow-up now ranging from 2 to more than 4 years. The company also reported no cases of 4D-150-related hypotony, endophthalmitis, or occlusive or non-occlusive retinal vasculitis to date.1 Voices from the field "Two-year PRISM data continue to strengthen our conviction in 4D-150's potential to become a foundational backbone therapy for wet AMD," said David Kirn, MD, co-founder, president, and CEO of 4DMT, in a company release. "The continued consistency in visual acuity and anatomic control with meaningful reduction in treatment burden and long-term tolerability reinforces our confidence in delivering a transformative treatment option for retina specialists and their patients."1 Awh, who presented the data at ASRS, framed the results in terms of the day-to-day burden that intensive anti-VEGF regimens place on both patients and practices. "For retina specialists and our patients, maintaining the intensive injection schedule necessary to preserve vision is a tremendous challenge," he said. "The two-year PRISM results demonstrate the potential of a single intravitreal administration of 4D-150 to provide long-term anti-VEGF and sustained disease control. Reducing treatment burden will undoubtedly improve our ability to preserve vision over the long term for our patients."1 Program context 4D-150 uses R100, a customized intravitreal AAV vector developed through 4DMT's proprietary Therapeutic Vector Evolution platform, to deliver sustained intraretinal expression of aflibercept and anti-VEGF-C from a single injection. The company positions the candidate as a potential "backbone" therapy across retinal vascular diseases, with wet AMD as the lead indication and diabetic macular edema (DME) as a second program , the latter supported by positive data from the SPECTRA trial.1,6 The two-year PRISM data arrive as 4DMT's Phase 3 wet AMD program moves toward readout. The company completed enrollment in 4FRONT-1 , its North American trial in treatment-naïve patients, earlier this year, with topline 52-week data expected in the first half of 2027. 4FRONT-2 , the global trial enrolling both treatment-naïve and recently diagnosed treatment-experienced patients, over-enrolled and completed ahead of schedule, with topline data anticipated in the second half of 2027.3,7 Both trials compare a single dose of 4D-150 against aflibercept 2 mg Q8W, with non-inferiority in BCVA change from baseline at 52 weeks as the primary endpoint and injection-count reduction as a key secondary endpoint.3 Wet AMD, in which abnormal blood vessels proliferate into the macula and leak fluid and blood under VEGF-driven stimulation, is projected to affect more than 4 million people across the US, EU, and Japan within five years, with roughly 200,000 new US diagnoses annually. Left untreated, the disease can progress to irreversible central vision loss.1 With durability data now extending past 2 years and Phase 3 readouts on the horizon, 4DMT continues to position 4D-150 as a candidate that could meaningfully reduce that burden for retina specialists and their patients. Optimize your guardrail policy against attacks the way you'd optimize a model against a loss
summary: In many working environments, fine-tuning a model simply is not an option. The model may be hosted or provided by a third party, or the cost, complexity, and governance requirements of retraining may rule it out.
body_text: Communications Santander CEST Linkedin Instagram X In many working environments, fine-tuning a model simply is not an option. The model may be hosted or provided by a third party, or the cost, complexity, and governance requirements of retraining may rule it out. When the weights cannot be changed, one of the most accessible levers is the policy or prompt around the model. The problem is that tuning that lever is usually a manual and time-consuming process. A few words are changed, the evaluations are run again, further edits are made, and the cycle repeats. Quite often, a small change that fixes one case quietly breaks behaviour that had already been secured. The result is a trial-and-error process with little experimental memory and poor scalability. Experience across different use cases within the bank repeatedly exposed this same pattern. That accumulated experience highlighted the value of a systematic way to search and optimize prompts and policies instead of relying on manual trial and error. That is the motivation behind autoguardrails — and the perspective that makes the rest of the design easier to understand. Search over policy.md, not train.py Autoguardrails is an alignment-research scaffold in the spirit of Karpathy's autoresearch. The difference lies in what gets optimized. While autoresearch searches over training code, autoguardrails searches over a single mutable surface: policy.md . Everything else (the evaluator, the attack suite, the judge) remains frozen. The guardrail policy is the only element that changes between runs. The objective is deliberately simple: Minimise attack success rate (ASR) - the fraction of adversarial prompts (jailbreaks, obfuscation, injection) that get through. Lower is better. Subject to a benign-pass floor - so the system can't cheat by refusing everything. A guardrail that blocks all traffic has an ASR of zero but is also useless. That second constraint is the key challenge. Driving attack success to zero is relatively easy if an assistant becomes overly restrictive; the difficult part is reducing attack success while still answering legitimate requests. To obtain that result the harness deliberately minimal: Python 3.10+, standard library only, offline by default. The loop is straightforward: establish a baseline, propose a candidate policy.md, measure its performance, and keep it only if it genuinely improved. # 1. establish a baseline against the fixed eval suite python -m autoguardrails baseline --reset --repeat 2 --notes "initial baseline" # 2. edit policy.md (the ONLY file you change between runs), then score it python -m autoguardrails candidate --repeat 2 --notes "cover jailbreak and obfuscation" # 3. see where things stand python -m autoguardrails status cat results.tsv The moving parts map cleanly onto files: policy.md — the only file you edit between runs; the guardrail policy, in prose. eval_suite.jsonl — the fixed set of attack and benign test cases. judge_prompt.md — the frozen judgment logic that decides pass/fail. results.tsv — an append-only log, so every experiment stays on the record. And we made the acceptance rule strict on purpose: keep a candidate only if ASR improves and benign-pass does not fall by more than 2 percentage points. That single line is the discipline made executable. It stops the classic failure mode where a policy tweak quietly trades away legitimate answers to look safer on paper. Pointing it at a real model By default, the system runs offline, but it can be connected to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Two separate sets of environment variables are used: one for the target model (the one being guarded) and one for the judge. export AUTOGUARDRAILS_TARGET_PROVIDER=... AUTOGUARDRAILS_TARGET_MODEL=... export AUTOGUARDRAILS_TARGET_API_BASE=... AUTOGUARDRAILS_TARGET_API_KEY=... export AUTOGUARDRAILS_JUDGE_PROVIDER=... AUTOGUARDRAILS_JUDGE_MODEL=... export AUTOGUARDRAILS_JUDGE_API_BASE=... AUTOGUARDRAILS_JUDGE_API_KEY=... Separating target and judge matters: the model under evaluation should not be responsible for grading its own defences. Why it is designed this way In practice, guardrail systems often evolve into collections of ad hoc rules that are difficult to evaluate. The idea here is to reframe the guardrail as a measurable artifact with an objective and a frozen benchmark . That's the only way improvements become real rather than moving goalpost. The policy is legible (prose in one file), the evaluation is fixed, and the log is append-only, so the history can't quietly disappear. In a regulated institution, those properties are particularly important. Transparency, traceability, and auditability are not optional extras; they are core requirements. It's also an honest scope as this idea is not claiming to have solved jailbreaks. Autoguardrails is a disciplined loop for making a policy measurably better against a fixed suite, while guarding against the “refuse everything” solution. Publishing the project openly also allows others to pressure-test the approach, identify weaknesses, and propose improvements rather than leaving the work confined to an internal drive. Run it, break it The purpose of opening the project is to make it usable, testable, and open to challenge. A good first exercise: swap eval_suite.jsonl for attacks that matter in a particular domain, set a benign-pass floor that reflects real requirements, and see how far a few careful edits to policy.md move the ASR. Finding where the system breaks is part of the value. Each failure can become a new evaluation case, a new hypothesis, and an opportunity to improve the policy. The next phase of AI will not be determined only by who has access to the most advanced technology, but by how responsibly, and how collectively that technology is built and shared. (Commands and file names above are quoted from the repo's README at the time of writing — check the repo for the current interface before running it)

title: The Recruiter Phone Screen: What They're Actually Filtering For (and How to Pass)
summary: A recruiter phone screen is a filter, not a deep interview. Here's what recruiters actually check, why salary sinks most screens, and how to pass the first round.
body_text: What is a recruiter phone screen actually for? It's a filter. A recruiter, usually not the hiring manager and rarely the technical expert, spends 15 to 30 minutes confirming you're worth the manager's time. They're checking a few boxes: do you really have the must-haves, does your salary number fit the budget, do you come across as easy to work with, and are you actually interested in this specific role. Nobody expects you to dazzle them on a screening call. You just need to avoid getting filtered out, so pass the boxes, keep it warm, and you move to the real interview. You applied, a resume made it through, and now a recruiter wants twenty minutes on the phone. Most people treat that call like a mini interrogation and psych themselves out. That's backwards. The phone screen is the lowest-stakes conversation in the whole hiring process, and the people who bomb it usually bomb it on one predictable thing, which is the salary question. Get that part right and you clear a bar most candidates trip over without ever knowing it was there. Quick disambiguation before we start. If the "call" is a chatbot texting you knockout questions, or a voice AI named Olivia running a scripted first round, that's a different animal with different rules. We covered that one separately in how to handle an AI screening call . This piece is about the human version: a real recruiter, a real conversation, and what they're quietly evaluating while you talk. The recruiter is a gatekeeper, not the decision-maker Here's the reframe that takes the pressure off. The recruiter on this call is almost never the person who decides whether you get hired. They work the top of the funnel. Their job is to hand the hiring manager a short list of people who clear the basics, and to filter out everyone who obviously doesn't fit before the manager wastes an hour. Which means a couple of things. The recruiter often can't judge the substance of your work. If you're an engineer, they're not going to test your system design; they're playing a matching game between the words on your resume and the words on the job description. They want to hear you say the thing that lets them tick the box. And because they're screening, not selling, the bar for passing is low. You don't fail a competent recruiter unless you genuinely lack the years they need, you're evasive on the deal-breakers, or you come across as someone nobody wants to sit next to. There's a second, more useful implication. When a screen goes fine and you still get a rejection a week later, you usually didn't fail the recruiter at all. The recruiter passed you along, and the hiring manager, looking at a stack of people, picked someone further down the pipeline they liked more. That's not a signal you did something wrong on the call. It's the volume math of a crowded market. Worth remembering the next time a "great conversation" goes nowhere. What they're actually filtering for Strip away the small talk and a phone screen is checking four things, roughly in this order. None of them is "how brilliant are you." Get them straight and you can prep for the call in about fifteen minutes instead of spiraling for a day. Each one gets its own section below. Filter one: the hard must-haves Do you actually have the things the requisition demands. The years of experience. The core skills. The certification, the license, the degree if the role requires one. Work authorization. And whether you can physically do the job where it's based, which means location, on-site days, remote eligibility, and travel. These get checked fast, sometimes in the first two minutes, and the recruiter is confirming them out loud even though your resume "already said so." Part of that is process. Part of it is that a human sometimes hasn't opened your resume until the call starts, because the software surfaced you and the recruiter is reading it live while you talk. Either way, this is where a call ends early when there's a hard mismatch. A recruiter who realizes you have one year of generalist experience for a role that needs three years of specialist work will thank you and hang up. It stings, but it saved you three more rounds. The move here is boring and effective: know the top three or four requirements in the posting cold, and be ready to confirm each in a sentence. If a must-have is a judgment call, like "5 years" when you have 4 doing exactly that work, say the real number and then bridge to why the work maps. Don't fudge the number. That's the one thing that gets caught later and kills the whole thing. Filter two: salary, the question that sinks most screens This is the one to prep for above all others. The recruiter will ask what you're expecting, and they'll usually ask early, because a compensation mismatch is the fastest way to end a call that would otherwise go nowhere. For a lot of recruiters it's the second question out of the gate, asked up front on purpose so nobody burns an afternoon on a number that was never going to work. People melt here. It happens over and over: someone with a clear target in their head opens their mouth and a lower number falls out, and they spend the next week sick about it. The fix is to decide your range before the phone rings and to give a range, not a single figure, with your real target sitting near the bottom of it so the whole band sounds reasonable. If a salary range is posted, treat it as real and calibrate inside it, because companies rarely hire at the top of a band; the top is there to leave room for raises. A few rules that hold up. Don't anchor on your current or past pay, and know that in a growing number of states, around twenty now, an employer isn't even allowed to ask what you make today. If you'd rather not name a number first, a composed deflection works: something like "based on my research the role sits around X to Y, and I'd want to weigh the full package before locking anything in." That signals salary isn't your only axis without stonewalling, which is the thing recruiters actually dislike. What they hate isn't a candidate who negotiates. It's a candidate who won't give them anything to work with, because they can't move you forward if they can't confirm you're in budget. One reassurance and one caution. Most recruiters will tell you the range if you ask, and plenty volunteer it before you do, precisely because they don't want to waste the call either. So asking "can you share the band for this role?" up front is normal and fine; frame it as saving everyone time and it lands well. The caution: a range on a posting can be soft, tiered, or wider than the real budget, so it's a guide, not a promise. The full script for handling this question, including the exact deflection and how to turn it around, lives in how to answer salary expectations . If you read one linked piece before your screen, read that one. Want to hear your salary answer out loud before the recruiter does? Run the "why are you leaving" and "what are you expecting" questions with Hiration's interview prep tool and get feedback before the call that counts. Practice your phone screen → Filter three: communication and quiet red flags Are you clear, coherent, and pleasant to deal with. That's most of it. Recruiters screen a lot of people, and a chunk of the filtering is simply confirming you're a normal person who can hold a professional conversation, because they're about to vouch for you to a manager and they don't want a surprise. A handful of things register as flags without you realizing. "Why are you looking to leave" is a trap if you answer "for more money," even though it's often true. To a recruiter that answer says you'll walk the moment someone offers a bigger bump, and the pay conversation is already handled on the screen anyway. Give a reason that isn't financial: growth, a scope you can't get where you are, a team or product you want to work on. Badmouthing your current employer reads the same way, as risk, so keep the exit story neutral even if the real story isn't. The other flag is being prickly. Recruiters ask softball rapport questions, and getting defensive about a light one, treating "what do you do outside work" like an invasion, does more damage than a boring answer ever would. You don't owe anyone your life story. You can pick what you share. But answer the question with something human and move on. The goal on every question, even the small ones, is a green flag, not a stalemate. Filter four: genuine interest and logistics Are you actually interested in this role, and can the practical stuff work. Availability, notice period, start date, whether you're fine with the on-site days, and sometimes whether you're interviewing elsewhere. A recruiter will also gauge whether you know the first thing about the company, because a lot of applicants spray one-click applications and can't say what the job even is once they're on the phone. Interest is easy to signal and easy to fumble. Have one or two concrete reasons this specific role fits, tied to something real in the posting, not "I'm passionate about the mission." And when the logistics come up late in a process, take it as a good sign rather than a nuisance. When a recruiter circles back to nail down notice period, days in office, and salary, that's usually the sound of you moving toward an offer, not a box being ticked for its own sake. Build a one-page screen sheet The whole call is predictable enough that you can prep it on a single page and keep it in front of you while you talk. Nobody can see it. Use it. Here's what belongs on it. The must-haves you meet. The top three or four requirements from the posting, each with your one-line confirmation, plus the honest number if any of them is a stretch. Your salary range. A researched band with your target near the bottom, and a one-line deflection in case you'd rather not go first. Availability. Notice period, earliest start, and whether the on-site or travel expectations work for you. Two reasons this role fits. Specific to this job, not generic enthusiasm. A crisp "why leaving." One non-money sentence you can say without thinking. Two questions to ask. About the role, the team, or the process. Not perks. That's it. Six things on one page. If a bot is running your first round instead of a person, the same sheet works there too, and we walk through that version in the AI screening piece linked up top. For the human call, the sheet does one more quiet thing: it keeps you concise, which matters more than you'd think. Keep it short, because they're on a clock Recruiters run these back to back, and a slot can be as short as fifteen minutes. So the fastest way to sabotage yourself is to ramble. The recruiter has a role to describe, three or four questions to get through, and time for yours, all inside that window. Monologue through one answer and the whole thing runs out before you reach the part that matters. The discipline is simple even when it doesn't feel natural: answer what they asked, add the single detail that actually earns its place, then stop talking. A beat of silence after a solid answer won't cost you anything. Let the recruiter steer. Then they'll hand you the last few minutes for your questions. Have two ready, no more, and make them worth asking. How the team is set up, what the first ninety days actually look like, why this seat came open, what the rest of the interview loop involves. Any of those tells the recruiter you're paying attention and hands you something you genuinely need to know. What you skip on a first call is the vacation-days-and-free-lunch stuff. That conversation has its place, later, once they've decided they want you. The recruiter is your ally, so treat them like one This is the part most candidates miss. A recruiter is not the enemy across the table. They are trying to fill this role, they get evaluated on filling it, and the fastest way for them to look good is to find someone who fits. When they like a candidate, they advocate. They carry your desired salary to the hiring manager and make the case. They coach you on what the manager cares about. They tell you what to lean on in the next round. A recruiter who's on your side is one of the most useful people in the whole process. You earn that by being easy to work with. Responsive to emails. Clear about your fit and your number. Warm on the phone. None of it is hard, and it costs nothing, and it's the difference between a recruiter who fights for you and one who quietly moves on. Because the flip side is just as real: flakiness, evasiveness on salary, arrogance, or being hard to reach gets you dropped without ceremony. They have a stack of other qualified people, and no obligation to chase you. If you make yourself the low-friction option, you win ties you didn't know were being played. One honest caveat. Not every recruiter is great, and agency recruiters in particular can have incentives that don't perfectly line up with yours. You'll run into the occasional one who's rude, who talks at you for thirty minutes without asking a question, or who lowballs on purpose. That's on them, and it's a data point about the company. But the existence of a few bad ones isn't a reason to treat all of them as adversaries. Being a good candidate is free and it pays off with the good ones, who are the majority. The logistics of the call itself Take the call seriously even though it's "just a phone call." That means somewhere quiet, with your resume, the job posting, and your screen sheet in front of you, and a note of the time zone so you're not off by an hour. Answer the phone like a professional, not with a distracted "yeah?" First impressions on a screen are audio-only, so tone and energy carry more weight than usual. Sound interested. Dial your energy up a notch from how you feel, because phone flattens it. Then there's the surprise call. A recruiter phones out of the blue and asks "is now a good time?" If you're genuinely not in a position to talk, it's completely fine to say "I'm about to head into something, could we do this later today or tomorrow?" and offer a specific window. But understand the tradeoff. When you're actively job hunting, you should assume any unknown number could be a recruiter, and they usually have plenty of other ready candidates. If you can step outside and take it now, that's often smarter than rescheduling and risking they just call the next person on the list. Be ready to give a decent version of "tell me about yourself" on zero notice, because that's the one you'll be asked. If what's scheduled is a video screen rather than a phone call, the rules shift, and the setup becomes part of the evaluation. Camera, lighting, background, and eye contact all start to matter. That's its own playbook, and we broke it down in how not to bomb a virtual interview . The most common ways people bomb a screen Almost every blown phone screen comes down to one of a handful of mistakes, and every one of them is avoidable. Winging the salary number is the big one; blurt a figure lower than you wanted, or refuse to give any number at all, and you've either capped yourself or given the recruiter nothing to move forward with. Rambling is next; eat the clock and the recruiter never gets to sell you or set up the next step. Then the softer ones. Sounding bored or low-energy, which reads worse on the phone than in person. Trashing your current employer, or answering "why are you leaving" with money. Not knowing what the company does, which instantly outs a spray-and-pray applicant. Being flaky, unreachable, or rescheduling three times, which tells a recruiter you'll be exactly this hard to manage as an employee. And getting defensive over routine logistics or rapport questions, which turns a nothing moment into a red flag. Notice that not one of these is about talent. They're all about handling. If you want the deeper cut on the specific questions that show up here, "why should we not hire you," "tell me about yourself," and the rest, with model answers, see our breakdown of the interview trap questions . And if the exit story is the part you're worried about, how to frame your reason for leaving is worth a read before you're put on the spot. After the screen, and what happens next When it's over, send a short thank-you within a day, keep it a couple of lines, name one thing from the conversation, and reaffirm you're interested. Then wait the way the recruiter told you to wait. If they gave you a timeline, hold to it and follow up a business day after it passes. If they didn't, about a week is the right cadence for a first nudge. The full timing, including how many follow-ups is too many, is in the follow-up timeline guide . A clean phone screen usually leads to one of two places: a recruiter-to-manager handoff, or the recruiter confirming logistics as you get closer to an offer. Both are good. If you want to see where the screen actually sits in the wider machine, from application to offer, our pillar on how hiring actually works maps every stage. The phone screen is early, it's low-stakes, and it's mostly won by preparation. Know your must-haves, know your number, keep it warm, and stop trying to wow anyone. You're just clearing the gate. Frequently Asked Questions How long does a recruiter phone screen usually last? Most run 15 to 30 minutes. Some recruiters book fifteen and move fast; others give themselves half an hour to explain the role and answer your questions. Treat it as short. That's exactly why rambling hurts you, the recruiter has a role overview, a few questions, and your questions to fit into a small window, and if you eat the clock the call never gets to the good part. Is the phone screen an actual interview? Not really. It's a filter that decides whether you're worth the hiring manager's time. The recruiter is confirming you have the must-haves, that your salary fits, and that you're easy to deal with. The real evaluation of your work happens later, with the manager and the team. So the goal here isn't to impress. It's to clear the basics without tripping over the salary question. What salary number should I give in a phone screen? Give a researched range, not a single figure, with your real target sitting near the bottom so the whole band sounds reasonable. Don't anchor on your current pay, and in a lot of states an employer can't legally ask for it anyway. If you'd rather not go first, a composed deflection about weighing the full package works. The complete script is in our guide on answering salary expectations . Can I ask the recruiter for the salary range up front? Yes, and most recruiters are fine with it. Plenty volunteer the band before you even ask, because they don't want to waste the call on a number that won't work either. Frame it as saving everyone's time, something like "can you share the range for this role so we know we're aligned," and it lands well. Just know a posted or quoted range can be soft, so treat it as a guide, not a locked promise. How do I answer "why are you leaving your current job"? With a reason that isn't money, even if money is part of it. To a recruiter, "for more pay" signals you'll leave again the second someone outbids them, and the comp conversation is already handled on the screen. Point to growth, scope, a team, or a product instead, and keep it neutral. Don't badmouth your employer. If you want it dialed in, see how to frame your reason for leaving . Is it possible to fail the recruiter screen specifically? Yes, but it's harder than people fear. You fail the recruiter directly if you clearly lack the years or skills the role needs, if you're evasive on a deal-breaker, or if you come across as someone nobody wants to work with. More often, the screen goes fine and you get rejected later because the hiring manager picked someone further along. That's the volume of a crowded market, not something you did wrong on the call. The recruiter called out of the blue and asked if now was a good time. What do I do? If you can take it, take it. When you're job hunting, treat any unknown number as a possible recruiter, and they usually have other ready candidates, so rescheduling carries a small risk. If you genuinely can't talk, it's fine to say "I'm about to head into something, could we do this later today?" and offer a specific time. Either way, keep a decent "tell me about yourself" ready to go on zero notice. What questions should I ask the recruiter? Have two ready, and keep them about the role, the team, or the process. Ask what the first ninety days look like, or why the role is open, or how many interview stages come after this one. Those get you information you genuinely need and they read as real interest at the same time. What you want to avoid is opening with vacation days and free lunch. There's a right moment to care about the perks, and it arrives after they've decided they want you, not thirteen minutes into a screening call. Is the recruiter on my side or evaluating me? Both at once, and the mix works in your favor. Yes they're filtering you, but they also get judged on filling the role, so when they like a candidate they push for them, carrying your salary number to the manager and prepping you for what comes next. The way you earn that is boring: reply to emails, be straight about your fit, don't be a pain to deal with. Get evasive or flaky or full of yourself and they'll quietly move to the next name on their list. What if an AI bot runs the first screen instead of a person? Then the rules shift. A chatbot firing knockout questions at you over text, or a voice AI reading from a script, isn't listening to your tone and won't go to bat for you later. It's matching your answers against filters. A lot of the prep carries over, since you still need your must-haves and your number ready, but the tactics are different enough that we gave it its own guide: how to handle an AI screening call . Everything on this page assumes a human is on the line. title: AI Stock Screener in 2026: Easy Platforms Compared
summary: Learn how AI stock screeners work and compare the top platforms in 2026. Find tools with AI analysis, stock ranking, real-time alerts, and smarter trading insights.
body_text: Finding the right AI stock screener can reshape how you identify trade opportunities across thousands of tickers. Whether you need real-time pattern recognition, natural-language queries, or multi-factor quantitative scoring, today's AI-driven tools deliver insights that manual filtering simply cannot match. In this guide, we break down the top platforms — including how to use an AI stock screener on desktop — so you can choose the tool that fits your trading style and goals. Table of Contents Part 1: What Is an AI Stock Screener and Why It Matters Part 2: AI Stock Screener Platforms for US Investors Part 3: How to Choose the Right AI Stock Screener FAQs The Bottom Line Part 1: What Is an AI Stock Screener and Why It Matters Defining the AI Stock Screener An AI stock screener is a software tool that uses machine learning models, natural language processing, and quantitative algorithms to filter, rank, and surface stock opportunities based on technical, fundamental, and alternative data inputs — going beyond static rule-based filters. Traditional screeners require you to manually set parameters: price range, P/E ratio, volume thresholds. An AI stock screener adds a predictive intelligence layer. It learns from historical price action, earnings surprises, institutional flow data, and market sentiment to surface opportunities you might never find with checkbox filters alone. How AI Screening Differs from Traditional Screening Feature Traditional Screener AI Stock Screener Filter logic Static, rule-based Dynamic, adaptive Data inputs Price, volume, ratios + Sentiment, flow, NLP signals Pattern recognition Manual chart review Automated ML detection Learning capability None Improves over time Natural language queries Not supported Supported on leading platforms Real-time adaptation Limited Continuous recalibration Why AI Screening Matters for Active Traders The US equity market lists over 8,000 stocks across NYSE, NASDAQ, and OTC markets. Manually scanning even a fraction of those tickers for momentum shifts, earnings catalysts, or unusual options activity is impractical. An AI stock screener compresses hours of research into seconds by: Detecting breakout patterns across multiple timeframes simultaneously Scoring stocks using multi-factor quantitative models Flagging unusual institutional or dark pool activity Analyzing earnings call transcripts and SEC filings via NLP Adjusting signal weighting based on current market regime (trending vs. mean-reverting) For investors managing diversified portfolios, this technology is no longer optional — it is a competitive baseline. Key Factors for Decision-Making Selecting an AI stock screener depends on your trading profile. title: Willow vs Wispr Flow Customer Success August 2026 | Willow
summary: Need the right dictation tool for your CS team? This August 2026 breakdown of Willow vs Wispr Flow covers speed, vocabulary accuracy, and team-level features.
body_text: Most dictation tools are built for one person writing in one place. Customer success teams don't work that way. You're across apps constantly, the terminology is account-specific, and the notes you take during a call have to be right the first time or you're editing instead of moving on. That gap between general-purpose dictation and what CS work actually demands is exactly what this Willow vs Wispr Flow for customer success breakdown is about. TLDR: Wispr Flow's ~700ms processing window works for general writing but can break rhythm in high-volume CS workflows. CS teams need domain vocabulary accuracy above all else; a tool that misses product names creates more rework than it saves. Wispr Flow adapts to general writing patterns but keeps each rep's corrections local, with no shared dictionary infrastructure. Both tools now hold SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA certifications, so compliance alone may not decide the choice for your team. One tool in this comparison runs at ~200ms, learns CS-specific vocabulary over time, and supports shared dictionaries across Mac, Windows, and iOS. Feature Willow Voice Wispr Flow Latency ~200ms ~700ms Device support Mac, Windows, iOS Mac (primary) Vocabulary learning Auto-Dictionary; learns over time passively Adapts to general writing patterns Shared team dictionary Yes, org-wide custom dictionaries Not available Admin controls Yes, org-wide deployment & user management Limited; individual-focused SOC 2 Type II Yes Yes HIPAA compliance Yes, with signed BAA HIPAA-eligible on certain plans Zero data retention Yes Not available Team leaderboards Yes Not available Best suited for CS teams needing consistent, org-wide vocabulary and fast latency Individual contributors doing general-purpose writing What Is Wispr Flow? Wispr Flow is a voice dictation tool built primarily for Mac users who want a fast, AI-assisted way to get words on screen without switching apps. It works system-wide, activating via a hold-to-talk mechanism, and uses AI to clean up speech into polished prose before the text lands in whatever field you're typing in. For a deeper look at how these two tools compare, see our Wispr Flow vs Willow breakdown. Where the Architecture Shows Its Limits Wispr Flow's design reflects a general-purpose use case. Its ~700ms processing window handles capture, transcription, interpretation, and formatting in a single pass, so text arrives later than a real-time engine. CS teams move constantly across CRM fields, support tickets, handoff notes, and email threads, and a tool optimized for polished prose in single-context writing behaves differently under that kind of multi-app load. What Is Willow Voice? Customer success work doesn't stay in one app. A CSM's day moves between CRM updates, Slack threads, call follow-ups, QBR decks, and renewal notes, often all before lunch. Learn how voice dictation for customer success can cut documentation time across these workflows. That context-switching is where documentation debt accumulates, and where a dictation tool either keeps up or becomes another source of friction. Willow Voice is built around that kind of work. A CSM recording a renewal summary or a post-call account note needs the text to land correctly the first time: the right product names, the right contact names, the right internal terminology, without a correction loop that costs more time than typing would have. Willow runs at ~200ms latency, works system-wide across every app a CSM touches, and learns vocabulary that matters to your team over time. Shared custom dictionaries standardize account names, product terminology, and internal shorthand org-wide, so every rep's notes transcribe consistently from day one. Available on Mac, Windows, and iOS, with SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA compliance, and admin controls built into how the product handles audio. Speed and Latency: Keeping Up With High-Volume Queues In customer success, the queue never really stops. Meeting follow-ups , escalation notes, CRM updates, renewal summaries, handoff briefs: the writing load compounds across every interaction, and the speed of your tools either keeps pace or becomes the bottleneck. Vitally's CS benchmarks find that 66% of CSMs spend a substantial portion of their day on repetitive administrative processes, a pattern where dictation speed directly affects net output. Wispr Flow processes at roughly ~700ms from the moment you stop speaking. That gap is noticeable when you're moving between tickets and adds up across a high-volume day. Willow runs at ~200ms. The difference goes beyond a spec on a comparison table: it determines whether the tool disappears into your workflow or interrupts it. See how Willow stacks up in our Whisper AI vs Willow speed breakdown. When you're capturing a renewal note while simultaneously tracking a live chat thread, a half-second lag pulls you out of context at exactly the wrong moment. Accuracy and Personalization for Customer Communication Wispr Flow handles general dictation capably, but customer success work carries a vocabulary load that general-purpose tools tend to underserve. Product names, internal feature terminology, customer account names, competitor references, acronyms your team invented three sprints ago: these terms show up in every call recap, follow-up email, and QBR summary. See how CSMs respond to support tickets faster with accurate dictation. Research on speech-to-text accuracy in specialized domains confirms that general-purpose ASR systems can drop sharply in performance when confronted with domain-specific vocabulary and industry jargon. When a tool doesn't recognize them, every document becomes a correction exercise. Where the Two Tools Differ Willow learns your vocabulary over time through its Auto-Dictionary, picking up names, technical terms, and contact references without manual setup. Shared custom dictionaries let teams standardize terminology across the org, so the product names and internal shorthand that one CSM uses transcribe consistently for every rep on the team. Wispr Flow adapts to general writing patterns but lacks a team-level vocabulary layer. Each rep's corrections stay local. For customer success teams where consistent language across accounts and handoffs matters, that gap tends to show up in the places it costs the most: escalation notes, renewal docs, and handoff summaries passed between reps. See how CSMs write client emails faster with Willow. Team Features and Enterprise Readiness Wispr Flow's team feature set is limited. There's no shared dictionary infrastructure, no admin controls for org-wide deployment, and no mechanism to carry one CSM's custom vocabulary to a new hire or a colleague on a different device. How Willow Approaches Team Deployment A customer success team logging notes across five CSMs needs those CSMs working from the same vocabulary baseline. Willow's shared custom dictionaries let teams standardize account names, product terminology, and internal shorthand org-wide, so "Churnzero," "NPS cycle," or a customer's branded product name transcribes consistently for every rep on Mac, Windows, or iOS. Admin controls give team leads visibility into adoption and configuration without per-seat manual setup. Team leaderboards surface usage and time-saved data across the group, so CS managers can see where voice input is taking hold and where onboarding support is needed, including for quick Slack updates that would otherwise pile up. On compliance: Willow is SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA certified, with a signed BAA available for teams operating in high-compliance industries. For CS teams working with healthcare or financial services accounts where data handling expectations are high, that infrastructure is already in place. Wispr Flow is now SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and HIPAA-eligible, so compliance alone may not separate the two tools for your team. The gap is in how team-level vocabulary, admin controls, and cross-device consistency are built into the deployment experience from the start, not left to individual configuration across a mixed-device org. Privacy, Compliance, and Data Controls When customer data lives inside every conversation, compliance becomes a workflow requirement. CS teams handle sensitive account details, renewal conversations, and escalation notes daily, and the tool transcribing those interactions needs to meet the same standards as the rest of your stack. Wispr Flow holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications and offers HIPAA eligibility on certain plans, covering a meaningful range of enterprise requirements. That covers a meaningful range of enterprise requirements, though it is not positioned as a purpose-built compliance tool with dedicated controls for heavily governed industry workflows. Willow Voice is SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant with a zero data retention architecture, and a Business Associate Agreement is available for organizations that need one. For a full breakdown, see our voice dictation privacy guide . Those aren't add-on tiers, they're built into how the product handles audio from the first keystroke. For CS teams at companies in healthcare, fintech, or any sector where account conversations carry regulatory weight, that distinction matters. Why Willow Voice Is the Better Choice for Customer Success Customer success runs on fast turnarounds. Unlogged churn signals, renewal notes that linger, follow-ups that never get sent: these are where accounts slip. The question with any dictation tool is whether it closes those gaps or creates new ones. Wispr Flow handles general-purpose voice input well enough for casual use, but customer success isn't casual. If you're comparing the best AI dictation tools across speed, accuracy, and enterprise readiness, that distinction matters. The vocabulary is specific: product names, account tiers, contract terms, internal escalation labels. A tool that hasn't learned that vocabulary makes you correct more than you capture. Where Willow Fits This Work When you voice a QBR summary or a churn risk note, Willow has already learned how your organization talks. Shared custom dictionaries carry terminology across the whole CS team, so an account name or product SKU transcribes correctly whether you set it up or a teammate onboarded last week. At ~200ms, text appears fast enough that your next thought stays intact; Wispr Flow's ~700ms compounds across a full call queue. Willow is SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant, supports Mac, Windows, and iOS across mixed-device teams, and gives CS leads visibility into adoption through team leaderboards. FAQs How does Willow Voice handle the specialized vocabulary that customer success work relies on? Willow's Auto-Dictionary learns product names, account names, internal terminology, and contact references over time without manual setup. Shared custom dictionaries let CS teams standardize that vocabulary across every rep, so a term one CSM sets up transcribes correctly for a teammate onboarded the following week, reducing the correction overhead on escalation notes, renewal docs, and account handoffs. Who is each tool best suited for? Wispr Flow works well for individual contributors who need polished prose from general dictation and work primarily within a single context. Willow Voice is built for customer-facing teams where consistent language across accounts, multi-app workflows, and enterprise requirements like SOC 2 Type II compliance and admin controls are part of the deployment reality. Does the latency difference between these two tools actually matter in day-to-day CS work? Yes, in high-volume queues it does. Willow runs at ~200ms, so text appears fast enough that your next thought stays intact. Wispr Flow processes at ~700ms, which is noticeable when you're moving between tickets or logging back-to-back interactions. That gap compounds across a full day of voicing renewal summaries, follow-up emails, and CRM updates. Final Thoughts on the Right Tools for Your CS Team If you're weighing Wispr Flow for customer success work, the straightforward answer is that it handles individual, general-purpose writing well. Where it falls short is at the team level: no shared vocabulary, no admin controls, and a ~700ms processing window that compounds across a full day of renewal notes and CRM updates. Team-level vocabulary consistency, faster latency, and org-wide admin controls are where Willow pulls ahead for CS workflows. Your notes, renewal summaries, and handoff briefs land correctly the first time, without a correction loop that costs more than typing would have. Download Willow Voice to put it to work across your team's stack.

title: FS KKR Capital Corp. Announces Second Quarter 2026 Results; Declares Third Quarter 2026 Distribution of $0.44 per share
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about FS KKR Capital Corp. 's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: PHILADELPHIA and NEW YORK , Aug. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FS KKR Capital Corp. (NYSE: FSK), or the Company, today announced its financial and operating results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and that its board of directors has declared a third quarter 2026 distribution of $0.44 per share for common stockholders. Financial and Operating Highlights for the Quarter Ended June 30, 2026 (1) Net investment income of $0.44 per share, compared to $0.42 per share for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 Adjusted net investment income(2) of $0.43 per share, compared to $0.41 per share for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 Net asset value of $18.30 per share as of June 30, 2026, compared to $18.83 per share as of March 31, 2026 Total net realized and unrealized loss of $0.56 per share, compared to a total net realized and unrealized loss of $2.00 per share for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 Adjusted net realized and unrealized loss(2) of $0.55 per share, compared to adjusted net realized and unrealized loss of $1.99 per share for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 Earnings (Loss) per share of ($0.13), compared to Earnings (Loss) per share of ($1.57) for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 Total purchases of $590 million versus $1,334 million of sales and repayments, including $9 million of net sales to the Company's joint venture, Credit Opportunities Partners JV, LLC Debt to equity ratio as of June 30, 2026 was 127%, compared to 138% as of March 31, 2026 Net debt to equity ratio(3) as of June 30, 2026 was 122%, compared to 131% as of March 31, 2026 Paid distributions to common stockholders totaling $0.42 per share(4) "During the second quarter, FSK generated Net Investment Income of $0.44 per share, reduced net leverage to within our target range, and made progress reducing our non-accrual assets," said Michael C. Forman, Chief Executive Officer and Chairman. "We remain focused on improving portfolio performance and delivering long-term value for shareholders." "The strategic actions we announced in May are progressing as planned and reflect the FS/KKR Advisor's continued conviction in the long-term value of FSK," said Daniel R. Pietrzak, President and Chief Investment Officer of FSK and Partner and Global Head of Private Credit at KKR. We believe these actions, together with our ongoing portfolio rotation efforts and focus on enhancing portfolio quality, strengthen FSK's financial profile." Subsequent Events During the period from July 1, 2026 through August 5, 2026, the Company repurchased 3,348,353 shares of common stock pursuant to the board-authorized share repurchase program at an average price per share (inclusive of commissions paid) of $10.75 (totaling $36 million). All such repurchases were made on the Company's behalf by a third-party agent on the open market at prices below net asset value per share in transactions intended to qualify for the safe harbors provided by Rules 10b5-1 and 10b-18 under the Exchange Act of 1934, as amended. The shares repurchased during the period from July 1, 2026 through August 5, 2026 are in addition to 377,800 shares of common stock (totaling $4 million at an average price per share, inclusive of commissions paid, of $10.57) repurchased from the commencement of the repurchase plan on June 29, 2026, through the end of the second quarter. title: Blue Ops, a Red Cat Company, and Havoc Partner to Develop Open-Architecture Autonomous Maritime Defense Systems
summary: Companies plan to integrate Havoc’s collaborative autonomy software across Blue Ops’ USV portfolio to establish operational fleets SALT LAKE…...
body_text: Blue Ops, a Red Cat Company, and Havoc Partner to Develop Open-Architecture Autonomous Maritime Defense Systems August 17, 2026 6:30am EDT Download as PDF Companies plan to integrate Havoc’s collaborative autonomy software across Blue Ops’ USV portfolio to establish operational fleets SALT LAKE CITY, Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Red Cat Holdings, Inc . (Nasdaq: RCAT) (“Red Cat” or the “Company”), a U.S.-based provider of advanced all-domain drone and robotic solutions for defense and national security, and Havoc , a leader in all-domain collaborative autonomy, announced a partnership today, formalized through Red Cat’s maritime division, Blue Ops. Under the partnership, Blue Ops and Havoc plan to integrate Havoc’s collaborative autonomy software and command-and-control capabilities across multiple Blue Ops uncrewed surface vessels, including the Variant 7 and additional platforms as they are introduced. The integration is intended to enable coordinated multi-vessel operations and expand the range of autonomous functions available to U.S. and allied defense customers. The partnership builds on Blue Ops’ Modular Open Systems Architecture (“MOSA”) approach to maritime systems, which is designed to support the rapid integration of autonomy, sensors, communications, payloads, and other mission technologies based on evolving operational requirements. Havoc’s collaborative autonomy technology has been successfully deployed on behalf of the U.S. Department of War in multiple operational contexts. “This partnership is exactly what our open-architecture strategy was built for,” said Barry Hinckley, President of Blue Ops. “Our goal is to build the best small USVs in the world while making it easy to integrate leading technologies from across the U.S. and our allies. Havoc has developed a powerful collaborative autonomy solution and integrating it with Blue Ops platforms gives customers greater choice and flexibility while accelerating how quickly advanced autonomous maritime capabilities can be fielded.” Blue Ops and Havoc also plan to establish operational fleets at Havoc’s headquarters in Rhode Island and Blue Ops’ headquarters in Florida. These locations will provide U.S. and allied defense customers and partners with access to integrated Blue Ops and Havoc systems for live demonstrations, testing, training and operational evaluation, including both single-vessel autonomy and coordinated multi-vessel operations. “Havoc’s primary strategy is to pair our leading-edge collaborative autonomy software with platform manufacturers who have already proven innovation, excellence, and scale,” said Paul Lwin, CEO and Co-Founder of Havoc. “Blue Ops is the perfect partner to continue our journey because they are building an open, flexible family of maritime systems that align directly with how we believe autonomy should be deployed. By integrating Havoc across the Blue Ops portfolio, we can give operators the ability to command and coordinate multiple autonomous vessels while preserving the flexibility to adapt as operational requirements evolve.” Additionally, the companies plan to work together to expand market access for their respective technologies. Blue Ops and Red Cat intend to introduce Havoc’s autonomy and command-and-control capabilities to their government and commercial customers, while Havoc intends to market Blue Ops’ family of USVs to its customer base. Together, the companies plan to pursue opportunities requiring integrated autonomous maritime systems. The partnership provides a framework for continued technical integration, demonstrations and joint customer engagement as the companies further develop their commercial relationship. About Red Cat Holdings, Inc. Red Cat (Nasdaq: RCAT) is a U.S.-based provider of advanced all-domain drone and robotic solutions for defense and national security. Through its integrated portfolio of trusted U.S. and allied hardware and software, Red Cat supports military, government, and public safety operations across air, land, sea and space. Its systems span small unmanned aircraft systems, uncrewed surface vessels, wireless power transfer technology, and autonomous swarming software to enhance situational awareness, operational effectiveness, and mission safety. Learn more at www.redcat.red . About Havoc Havoc is a leader in all-domain collaborative autonomy. Its software-defined hardware approach powers military and commercial-grade autonomous systems across sea, air, and land to sense, decide, and act together in complex and contested environments. Havoc connects assets, enabling them to share information, adapt in real time, and continue operating even when communications are disrupted or denied. Havoc optimizes mission performance and minimizes human risk. Learn more at havocai.com. title: e-STORAGE's KuBank 3.0 for C&I Applications Successfully Passes Large-Scale Fire Testing
summary: KITCHENER, ON, Aug. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canadian Solar Inc. (the "Company" or " Canadian Solar ") (NASDAQ: CSIQ) today announced that e-STORAGE, its energy storage solutions business, has successfully completed Large-Scale Fire Testing (LSFT) for its KuBank 3.0 commercial and industrial (C&I)
body_text: KITCHENER, ON , Aug. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canadian Solar Inc. (the "Company" or "Canadian Solar") (NASDAQ: CSIQ) today announced that e-STORAGE , its energy storage solutions business, has successfully completed Large-Scale Fire Testing (LSFT) for its KuBank 3.0 commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage system under the latest UL 9540A:2026 standard, becoming the industry's first to pass this rigorous large-scale fire test. KuBank 3.0 delivers up to 940 kWh of energy capacity in a single liquid-cooled cabinet. Built with advanced 314 Ah LFP battery cells, it supports flexible 400V, 690V, and 800V architectures, offers integrated load connection, enables seamless transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, and holds comprehensive international certifications. The LSFT is a rigorous system-level safety evaluation designed to assess how an energy storage system behaves under extreme fire conditions, including whether fire can be contained within the tested unit and prevented from propagating to adjacent systems. For customers, this validation is critical because it provides third-party visibility into fire safety performance, supports permitting and project approval processes, and helps reduce deployment risk in C&I environments. Conducted under highly demanding conditions, the test evaluated a fully charged 940 kWh system with thermal runaway intentionally initiated and all fire suppression systems disabled. During the approximately four-hour fire event, no explosion occurred, the cabinet structure remained intact, and no fire propagation was observed in neighboring units. KuBank 3.0 passed the test on its first attempt without corrective actions, validating its advanced safety performance under the latest UL 9540A:2026 standard. The test was witnessed and independently verified by both TÜV Rheinland , the testing agency, and Energy Safety Response Group (ESRG) , a fire safety consultant. Designed with an independent physical compartment architecture, high-strength fire-resistant construction, and advanced thermal insulation materials, KuBank 3.0 enhances fire safety performance at the system level. Its intelligent liquid-cooling system maintains battery temperatures within the optimal operating range with a temperature deviation of ≤3°C, while its multi-layer active safety architecture integrates zone isolation, early thermal runaway monitoring, multi-stage fire detection, and protection technologies to support safe and reliable operation. Jeff Roy, President of e-STORAGE, said, "Passing this large-scale fire test on the first attempt demonstrates the strength of KuBank 3.0's safety-first design. As safety standards continue to evolve, customers need energy storage solutions that have been validated under the most demanding real-world conditions. This achievement provides greater confidence in the safe deployment of KuBank 3.0 across C&I applications." KuBank 3.0 has entered mass production and is now available to customers worldwide. About TÜV Rheinland As a leading global testing and certification body, TÜV Rheinland provides technical services that support the green energy transition. With a focus on reliability, innovation, and sustainability, TÜV Rheinland helps the industry address technical challenges and establish high-quality standards. About Energy Storage Response Group (ESRG) ESRG is a U.S.-based consulting firm specializing in battery energy storage system (BESS) safety, fire protection, and regulatory compliance. Backed by experienced fire service professionals and engineers, ESRG provides technical consulting, risk assessment, permitting support, and emergency response planning, helping manufacturers, developers, utilities, and regulators deploy energy storage systems safely and in compliance with industry standards. About Canadian Solar Inc. Canadian Solar is one of the world's largest solar technology and renewable energy companies. Founded in 2001 and headquartered in Kitchener, Ontario, the Company is a leading manufacturer of solar photovoltaic modules; provider of solar energy and battery energy storage solutions; and developer, owner, and operator of utility-scale solar power and battery energy storage projects. Over the past 25 years, Canadian Solar has successfully delivered nearly 177 GW of premium-quality, solar photovoltaic modules to customers across the world. Through its subsidiary e-STORAGE, Canadian Solar had shipped over 20 GWh of battery energy storage solutions to global markets as of March 31, 2026, and had a $3.5 billion contracted backlog as of May 8, 2026. Since entering the project development business in 2010, Canadian Solar has developed, built, and connected approximately 12.2 GWp of solar power projects and 6.4 GWh of battery energy storage projects globally. Its geographically diversified project development pipeline includes 24 GWp of solar and 81 GWh of battery energy storage capacity in various stages of development. Canadian Solar is one of the most bankable companies in the solar and renewable energy industry, having been publicly listed on the NASDAQ since 2006. For additional information about the Company, follow Canadian Solar on LinkedIn or visit www.canadiansolar.com . About e-STORAGE e-STORAGE is a subsidiary of Canadian Solar and a leading company specializing in designing, manufacturing, and integrating battery energy storage systems for utility-scale applications. e-STORAGE offers proprietary battery energy storage systems (BESS) spanning battery cells, battery PACKs, power conversion systems (PCS), energy management systems (EMS) and system integration. It also provides comprehensive EPC services and full-lifecycle station operation and asset management, helping customers improve grid operations across the project lifecycle. For more info, please refer to the Media&PR section of www.csestorage.com and follow our LinkedIn page.
